statutory.question: Does the conduct described fall within 31 U.S.C. § 5324 — Structuring transactions to evade reporting requirements?
statutory.answer: Insufficient facts to determine whether 31 U.S.C. § 5324 applies; § 5324 prohibits structuring to evade reporting requirements, but the record does not show intent to evade or a pattern of breaking up a single reportable cash transaction.
statutory.label: neutral
statutory.reasoning: 31 U.S.C. § 5324 prohibits (among other things) structuring or attempting to structure a transaction with a domestic financial institution for the purpose of evading Bank Secrecy Act reporting requirements (e.g., CTR reporting for currency transactions over $10,000). To apply § 5324, the facts must support: (1) a reportable transaction (typically currency > $10,000, or multiple related currency transactions treated as one) that would trigger a reporting requirement; (2) the defendant structured/assisted/attempted to structure transactions; and (3) the purpose/intent was to evade the reporting requirement. Here, the fact pattern shows many cash transactions, including numerous single cash transactions above $10,000 (e.g., $18,187.03; $12,946.10; $12,786.86; $10,077.29; $11,286.31; $19,880.06; $13,337.60; $18,289.77; $19,062.11; $17,342.62). Those amounts suggest CTR-triggering events rather than sub-$10,000 “breakups,” and the record does not indicate any same-day or closely related cash deposits/withdrawals split into amounts below $10,000 to avoid reporting. Critically, § 5324 requires an evasion purpose; the provided notes/metadata do not show intent to evade, instructions to avoid CTRs, use of multiple branches/accounts to stay under thresholds, or other indicia of structuring. Therefore, while the activity may implicate BSA reporting generally, the elements of § 5324 (especially intent to evade via structuring) are not established on these facts.
